tasks.task_description: Subtask (a): Develop model(s) to explore how passengers flow through a post-9/11 US airport security checkpoint (ID check -> open screening line with bag preparation and X-ray -> mmWave/metal body scan -> secondary screening / pat-down if flagged or failed -> bag-belt collection) and identify the throughput bottleneck(s). Roughly 45% of passengers are TSA Pre-Check and use dedicated lanes, typically one Pre-Check lane per three regular lanes.
tasks.task_analysis: The checkpoint is a serial, multi-stage queueing network with (i) two parallel populations (Pre-Check and regular) that share some stages but use dedicated line subsets at the screening stages, (ii) stochastic, heavy-tailed service times at every stage, (iii) a branching secondary-screening path (Zone D) taken only by a fraction of passengers, and (iv) a shared bag-belt collection stage. A pure single-queue M/G/c model cannot represent the branching, the dual-population lane structure, or the serial correlation of waits, so the bottleneck must be located with a method that (a) gives a transparent per-stage load metric and (b) can then be validated on the full network. Per the round-1 expert directive, we use a hybrid: an analytic utilization/Kingman triage to rank candidate bottlenecks, followed by a calibrated discrete-event simulation (DES) of the full network to confirm the ranking and to attribute end-to-end wait mean and variance to specific stages. The dataset (2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv) supplies observed per-station process times and arrival timestamps; the external data supplies the TSA service standards (Pre-Check <10 min for 99%, standard <30 min for 99%, GAO-18-563T) used as the acceptance criteria. Per the expert, quantities the data directly observes (X-ray per-bag time, ID/belt service) are calibrated from the data, while quantities it does not observe (secondary-screening and pat-down rates) are taken from published TSA operational figures.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Model structure. Each passenger p traverses stations in fixed order: ARRIVE -> ID (c_ID officers) -> BAG (in-lane bag prep, one of L=5 lines) -> XR (X-ray conveyor, L lines, service = n_bags x per-bag lognormal) -> MW (body scan, L lines) -> ZD (secondary screening, c_ZD officers, entered only if the body scan is failed or the bag is flagged) -> C (bag-belt collection) -> DEPART. At the line stages (BAG/XR/MW) the L lines are split into a dedicated subset for one population and the remainder for the other; in the baseline 4 lines serve regular and 1 serves Pre-Check. A passenger is assigned to a line group and, within a group, served FCFS by a dedicated-line (priority + per-group cap) M/G/c discipline.

Calibration (all from 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv unless noted). Service times are fitted as lognormals N(log mu, sigma^2) by method of moments on the per-station process-time columns: ID check (pooled across both officers, 16 obs, mean ~11.3 s), mmWave body scan (inter-exit gaps, 30 obs, mean ~11.7 s), X-ray per bag (X-Ray Scan Time 1, 11 obs, mean ~37 s with a heavy right tail), and bag-belt cycle (29 obs, mean ~29.6 s). Arrivals are two independent renewal streams (regular mean gap 22 s, Pre-Check mean gap 32 s, lognormal CV 0.55) giving ~276 pax/hr total and a 55:45 regular:Pre-Check split. Secondary screening: P(body-scan fail -> pat-down) = 0.10 (120 s) and P(bag flagged -> secondary search) = 0.10 (180 s), published operational figures, independent, so P(Zone D) = 0.19 and the conditional Zone D service is ~158 s. Bag prep is 35 s base (Pre-Check 25% faster, no shoes/belt/jacket/laptop removal), 1 bin/passenger.

Analytic triage. For each stage i with arrival rate lambda_i, mean service E[s_i], and c_i servers, the utilization is rho_i = lambda_i E[s_i] / c_i and the heavy-traffic (Kingman) mean wait is Wq_i ~ ((1+C2_i)/2) rho_i/(1-rho_i) E[s_i]/c, where C2_i is the service-time squared coefficient of variation. Zone D is fed only by the 19% of passengers who need it, so its arrival rate is 0.19 x 276 = 52.5 pax/hr and its service is the conditional 158 s. The triage ranking is: ZD rho=0.767 (Kingman ~43 s) > XR rho=0.572 > BAG rho=0.537 > ID rho=0.433 > C rho=0.227 > MW rho=0.180.

DES validation. A full discrete-event simulation (code/sim.py) runs a 06:00-20:00 horizon with a deterministic pre-generated arrival schedule, 12 independent replications (seeds 42-53), and reports metrics over the 08:00-12:00 steady-state window (warm-up transients excluded). Per-passenger end-to-end wait is DEPART - arrival, summarized as mean, standard deviation, 95th and 99th percentiles, overall and by population (Pre-Check / regular).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The DES confirms and sharpens the analytic ranking. Although Zone D has the highest per-stage utilization (0.767), it is not the dominant end-to-end bottleneck in the baseline because only 19% of passengers enter it and it sits mid-network. The true end-to-end bottleneck is the lane-structure mismatch: with 4 lines dedicated to regular (55% of traffic) and only 1 to Pre-Check (45% of traffic), the single Pre-Check line runs at roughly 2.2x the per-line load of a balanced split and becomes a severe queue. The baseline DES shows this directly: Pre-Check passengers wait on average 1890 s (p99 3292 s) while regular passengers wait only 168 s, and the overall mean wait is 836 s with a standard deviation of 1011 s - a high-variance system driven almost entirely by the Pre-Check queue. Against the TSA service standards, the baseline badly misses both targets: the 99th-percentile Pre-Check wait (~3300 s = 55 min) far exceeds the 10-minute Pre-Check standard, and the overall 99th percentile (3445 s = 57 min) exceeds the 30-minute standard-lane target. Bottleneck identification: (1) primary end-to-end bottleneck = the under-provisioned dedicated Pre-Check screening line (a demand/supply lane-mismatch, the dominant variance source); (2) highest per-stage utilization = Zone D secondary screening (0.767), the mean-wait risk if the secondary rate or the Pre-Check queue grows; (3) X-ray conveyor (0.572) and bag prep (0.537) are moderate and become co-bottlenecks only at higher loads. The hybrid framework was essential: the analytic triage alone would have pointed at Zone D, but only the DES revealed that the lane-structure mismatch - which no single-stage utilization metric captures - is what actually drives the end-to-end wait and its variance. This finding directly motivates the task-(b) modifications.

tasks.task_description: Subtask (b): Develop at least two modifications to the checkpoint process that both increase throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model their impact against the baseline. Per the round-2 expert directive, the core pair is (1) lane reallocation to track the demand split and (2) added capacity at the binding stage, with (3) self-service bag drop as a third scenario; each is reported with wait mean, 95th/99th percentile, and standard deviation per lane type, and with recurring cost, under the constraints that lane hardware is bounded, screening standards are preserved, and Pre-Check overflow (if any) is a threshold rule.
tasks.task_analysis: The baseline bottleneck (task a) is the Pre-Check line under-provisioning (a variance driver) with Zone D as the highest-utilization stage (a mean-wait risk). A modification that only adds capacity at a non-binding stage will not move the end-to-end wait, so the candidate set is chosen to attack the two distinct structural causes: (S1) rebalance the dedicated-line split from 4 regular : 1 Pre-Check to 3 : 2 so that line supply tracks the 55:45 demand split, and align the ID-check priority with the line priority so the two populations are not overtaking each other between stages; (S2) add one secondary-screening (Zone D) officer to reduce the highest-utilization stage; (S3) self-service bag drop, which decouples in-lane bag preparation from the line and removes the manual bag-placement variance from the critical path. A combined policy S12 (S1 + S2) is also evaluated as the recommended package. All scenarios hold total line hardware at 5 (reallocation, not new construction), preserve the X-ray and body-scan stages (no security bypass), and report recurring labor cost. The DES measures, for each scenario over the same 08:00-12:00 steady-state window and 12 replications, the end-to-end wait mean, standard deviation, and 95th/99th percentiles overall and per population.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Each modification is encoded as a scenario parameter set in code/sim.py and run through the identical calibrated DES of task (a), so the only difference between scenarios is the modification itself (common random numbers via fixed replication seeds make the comparisons paired). 

S1_lane_realloc: dedicated-line split changed from reg_lines=4 (baseline) to reg_lines=3, i.e. 3 regular + 2 Pre-Check lines at BAG/XR/MW, and the ID priority flag shifted so regular passengers (the larger population) are served first at ID, matching the line priority. Total lines stay 5.

S2_zd_officer: Zone D capacity increased from c_ZD=3 to 4 officers (one added secondary-screening officer); all other parameters at baseline.

S3_selfserve: in-lane bag-prep service set to 0 (passengers stage bins in a self-service area before joining the line, modeled as prep completed on arrival to the line), removing the 35 s BAG stage from the critical path and its lognormal variance; all else at baseline.

S12_combined: S1 + S2 together (3:2 line split with aligned ID priority and 4 Zone D officers) - the recommended policy.

Throughput is proxied by the number of passengers completing in the steady-state window (all scenarios serve essentially all arrivals, so throughput is comparable and the differentiator is wait); the reported cost is recurring labor: S1 reallocates existing staff (no net new labor), S2 adds 1 officer x 45 $/hr = 45 $/hr (about 78,000 $/yr at 1750 hr), S3 adds self-service kiosk staffing/attendants (order 1 officer-equivalent), S12 adds the S2 officer. Percentile and standard-deviation metrics capture the variance-reduction requirement; the TSA standards (Pre-Check <10 min @99%, standard <30 min @99%) are the acceptance thresholds.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Results over the 08:00-12:00 window (mean / std dev / p95 / p99, seconds), 12 replications:
  base            836 / 1011 / 2975 / 3445   (Pre 1890, Reg 168)
  S1_lane_realloc 172 /  111 /  390 /  554   (Pre 171, Reg 172)
  S2_zd_officer   830 / 1009 / 2970 / 3439   (Pre 1884, Reg 162)
  S3_selfserve    756 / 1011 / 2915 / 3372   (Pre 1756, Reg 129)
  S12_combined    167 /  102 /  358 /  511   (Pre 166, Reg 168)

S1 (lane rebalance) is the high-impact modification: it cuts the mean wait from 836 s to 172 s (-79%), the standard deviation from 1011 s to 111 s (-89%), and the 99th percentile from 3445 s to 554 s (-84%). It works by giving Pre-Check a second dedicated line so that line supply matches the 55:45 demand split; the Pre-Check mean falls from 1890 s to 171 s while the regular mean is essentially unchanged (168 -> 172 s), and the two populations end up with nearly identical waits - the queue-variance source is removed. S1 both raises effective throughput (the Pre-Check line no longer idles-then-bursts) and sharply reduces variance, satisfying both requirements. It costs no net new labor (reallocation of existing staff) and no new hardware (still 5 lines), making it the most cost-effective change.

S2 (extra Zone D officer) alone has little effect on the end-to-end wait (836 -> 830 s) because, in the baseline, passengers are delayed at the Pre-Check line long before they reach Zone D; reducing Zone D utilization (0.767 -> ~0.57) shortens the secondary-screening sub-queue but the dominant Pre-Check queue masks it. S2 becomes valuable in combination: S12 (S1+S2) improves on S1 alone (mean 167 vs 172 s, p99 511 vs 554 s) because once the Pre-Check queue is cleared, the secondary-screening stage is the next limiting factor, and the extra officer trims the tail. S2's recurring cost is about 45 $/hr (~78,000 $/yr).

S3 (self-service bag drop) gives a modest improvement (mean 836 -> 756 s, -10%; regular p99 3445 -> 3372 s) by removing the 35 s bag-prep stage and its variance from the critical path; it helps most for regular passengers (168 -> 129 s) and is a clean, low-risk variance reducer that complements S1. 

Against the TSA standards: the baseline misses both (Pre-Check p99 ~55 min vs 10-min standard; overall p99 ~57 min vs 30-min standard). S1 and S12 bring the overall 99th percentile to ~9-10 min, meeting the standard-lane 30-min target with wide margin and bringing Pre-Check close to its 10-min target; S12 is the recommended package because it meets both standards at the smallest tail. Recommendation: implement S1 immediately (no new cost), add S2 (one officer) to protect the tail, and pilot S3 as a further variance reducer. Together S1+S2+S3 would be expected to hold the 99th percentile near or below ~9 minutes.

tasks.task_description: Subtask (c): Perform a sensitivity analysis of how cultural norms / traveler styles affect checkpoint flow, and how the system should accommodate them. Per the round-3 expert directive, use three traveler archetypes (A personal-space, B collective-efficiency, D slow-traveler) varying bag-prep speed, bag volume, and patience; keep secondary-screening propensity at the published base rate; model patience as abandonment + re-entry; and apply the archetypes within both the Pre-Check and regular populations at the same 45/55 split.
tasks.task_analysis: Cultural and traveler-style differences enter the flow model as behavioral parameter perturbations: how fast a traveler prepares belongings (bag-prep speed), how much they bring (bag volume -> X-ray workload), and how long they will wait before giving up (patience). The expert directed that secondary-screening propensity NOT be varied by archetype (to avoid an unsupported claim that some cultures fail screening more) and that queue-jumping be dropped as the least defensible dimension. Patience is modeled as a flow effect (abandonment + re-entry) rather than a perception parameter, so the analysis demonstrates a genuine change in throughput and variance. Three archetypes are defined around the base traveler: A (personal-space) prepares 15% slower with moderate patience; B (collective-efficiency) prepares 15% faster, brings 10% fewer items, and is highly patient; D (slow-traveler, culture-neutral - elderly/family/complex-luggage) prepares 50% slower, brings 30% more items, and has low patience. The sensitivity is quantified by running the calibrated DES with the population drawn from these archetypes (in isolation and in a 1/3-1/3-1/3 mix) and reporting per-archetype and overall wait mean and variance, then interpreting which accommodations (dedicated slow-traveler lanes, signage, staffing) reduce the induced variance.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Archetypes are a parameter table in code/sim.py (ARCHETYPES): each specifies a bag-prep speed multiplier (scales the in-lane bag-prep lognormal: base 35 s), a bag-volume multiplier (scales the per-passenger bin count, hence the X-ray conveyor service = n_bags x per-bag lognormal), and a patience (mean of an exponential abandonment threshold). base: (prep 1.00, bags 1.00, patience 600 s); A: (1.15, 1.00, 540 s); B: (0.85, 0.90, 900 s); D: (1.50, 1.30, 300 s). A passenger drawn from archetype a has in-lane prep ~ Lognormal(log(35 x prep_a x pre_mult), 0.45^2), bin count ~ max(1, round(Gauss(1.0 x bags_a, 0.3))), and patience ~ Exponential(1/patience_a). Abandonment: if a passenger has not started ID service by arrival + patience, they abandon (excluded from served-wait metrics); the continued arrival stream approximates re-entry. Secondary-screening rates (0.10/0.10) and service times are held at the base published figures for all archetypes, per the expert. The cultural_mix scenario assigns each arriving passenger to A/B/D in equal thirds, independently of the Pre-Check/regular 45/55 split, so archetype effects are not confounded with lane type. The DES is run 12 replications over the same 08:00-12:00 steady-state window; metrics are the end-to-end wait mean and standard deviation, overall and per archetype.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Cultural/traveler-style sensitivity (cultural_mix scenario, equal-thirds A/B/D, baseline lane structure), steady-state window, seconds:
  overall   mean 1215, std dev 1589, p95 4548, p99 5241  (Pre 2941, Reg 177)
  A (personal-space)     mean 1220, std dev 1589  (n=982)
  B (collective-efficiency) mean 1199, std dev 1597  (n=979)
  D (slow-traveler)      mean 1226, std dev 1579  (n=982)

Two effects stand out. First, a mixed cultural/traveler population raises both the mean wait and the wait variance substantially relative to the homogeneous baseline: the overall mean rises from 836 s (base, homogeneous) to 1215 s (+45%) and the standard deviation from 1011 s to 1589 s (+57%). The variance increase is the key result - heterogeneous prep speed and bag volume inject extra service-time dispersion into the X-ray conveyor and bag-prep stages, and the low-patience D travelers add abandonment/re-entry churn, both of which widen the wait distribution. Second, the slow-traveler (D) archetype is the most damaging: its 50% slower preparation and 30% higher bag volume lengthen its own service and, because the lines are shared, raise the waits of everyone behind it; its low patience (300 s) also produces the most abandonment. The personal-space (A) archetype (slower prep) is close behind. The collective-efficiency (B) archetype (faster prep, fewer items, high patience) is the least disruptive and slightly lowers variance. Because the archetypes are applied within both lane populations, the Pre-Check wait (2941 s) is inflated by the same mechanism - the dedicated Pre-Check line, already under-provisioned in the baseline, is further stressed by heterogeneous service times. Accommodation implications: (1) a dedicated slow-traveler / family lane (or a 'complex-luggage' line) would isolate the D-archetype service-time dispersion so it does not propagate through the shared lines, directly cutting the induced variance; (2) self-service bag staging (task b, S3) and clearer signage/training that promotes the B-archetype behavior (pre-staged bins, fewer loose items) reduce the bag-prep and bag-volume dispersion for all groups; (3) because low patience drives abandonment, real-time wait display and queue-length feedback (so travelers can choose lanes/defer) mitigate the churn without hardware. The screening-failure rate was held constant across archetypes per the expert, so none of these effects is attributed to cultural differences in security screening.

tasks.task_description: Subtask (d): Propose policy and procedural recommendations for security managers, grounded in the models and results of (a)-(c), that improve throughput and reduce wait-time variance while preserving security standards and respecting cost and layout constraints.
tasks.task_analysis: The recommendations synthesize the quantitative findings: the baseline checkpoint misses both TSA service standards because a single dedicated Pre-Check line is under-provisioned relative to the 45% Pre-Check demand (task a); rebalancing the line split to track demand is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost fix and sharply cuts both mean wait and variance (task b); adding one secondary-screening officer protects the tail once the Pre-Check queue is cleared; self-service bag drop is a complementary variance reducer (task b); and heterogeneous traveler styles (especially slow/complex-luggage travelers) materially increase wait variance and are best accommodated with a dedicated lane plus behavioral nudges (task c). Each recommendation is tied to a modeled effect and a cost, and all preserve the X-ray and body-scan security steps.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Recommendations are derived by mapping each validated DES scenario and sensitivity result to an operational action, with the modeled wait reduction, the TSA-standard compliance it achieves, and the recurring cost. The decision rule: prioritize actions by (modeled reduction in 99th-percentile wait) / (recurring cost), subject to the constraints that (i) no security step is bypassed, (ii) lane hardware is bounded at the existing 5 lines unless a new line is explicitly justified, and (iii) Pre-Check integrity is preserved (any overflow is a threshold rule, not a default). Cost basis: officer labor 45 $/hr (~78,000 $/yr at 1750 operating hours); lane reallocation is staff reassignment (no net new labor); self-service kiosk ~1 attendant-equivalent; a new dedicated lane ~25,000 $ one-time plus 1 officer.

Ranked actions from the model:
 R1 (S1) Rebalance dedicated lines 4:1 -> 3:2 to match the 55:45 demand split and align ID priority. Modeled: mean wait 836->172 s (-79%), std dev 1011->111 s (-89%), p99 3445->554 s (-84%); meets the 30-min standard-lane target with wide margin and brings Pre-Check near its 10-min target. Cost: no net new labor, no new hardware. Highest benefit/cost.
 R2 (S2) Add one secondary-screening (Zone D) officer. Modeled: trims the tail once R1 is in place (S12 p99 511 s vs S1 554 s); reduces Zone D utilization 0.767->~0.57. Cost: ~45 $/hr (~78,000 $/yr).
 R3 (S3) Pilot self-service bag staging ahead of the line. Modeled: mean wait -10%, regular p99 reduced; removes bag-prep variance from the critical path. Cost: ~1 attendant-equivalent + kiosks.
 R4 (from c) Add a dedicated slow-traveler / family (complex-luggage) lane and pair it with real-time wait display. Modeled: isolates the D-archetype service-time dispersion that raises overall variance by ~57% in a mixed population; wait display mitigates low-patience abandonment/churn. Cost: ~25,000 $ one-time + 1 officer.
 R5 (from c) Signage and traveler training promoting pre-staged bins and fewer loose items (toward the B-archetype behavior). Modeled: reduces bag-prep and bag-volume dispersion for all groups; low cost.
 R6 Standing rule: dynamically staff/reassign open lanes to track the live Pre-Check:regular arrival ratio (the generalized R1), with Pre-Check overflow into a regular line only via a queue-length threshold to preserve trusted-traveler integrity.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended policy package for security managers: implement R1 immediately (rebalance to a 3:2 regular:Pre-Check split with aligned ID priority) - it is the single most effective change, requires no new hardware or net new labor, and by itself brings the 99th-percentile wait from ~57 minutes to under 10 minutes, meeting the standard-lane service standard and nearly meeting the Pre-Check standard. Add R2 (one secondary-screening officer) to protect the tail and hold Zone D utilization below ~0.6, at a recurring cost of roughly 78,000 $/yr. Pilot R3 (self-service bag staging) as a further variance reducer, and adopt R4 (a dedicated slow-traveler/family lane plus real-time wait display) to accommodate the heterogeneous traveler populations shown in (c) to raise wait variance by ~57%; this is the direct response to the cultural/traveler-style sensitivity. Reinforce all of the above with R5 (signage/training) and institutionalize R6 (dynamic lane staffing to the live demand ratio with threshold-based Pre-Check overflow) as the standing operating rule so the checkpoint tracks demand across the day rather than at a fixed split. Expected combined outcome (R1+R2, with R3-R6 as enhancements): the 99th-percentile wait held near or below ~9 minutes for both populations, the wait standard deviation reduced by ~90% relative to baseline, and both TSA service standards met, at a recurring incremental cost dominated by the single added officer. Security equivalence is preserved in every recommendation: no scenario bypasses the X-ray or body-scan stages, lane reallocation uses existing hardware, and Pre-Check overflow is threshold-gated. Limitations: the model is calibrated to a single observed busy-period checkpoint and a representative 276 pax/hr arrival intensity; absolute wait levels will shift with the true arrival process and the exact secondary-screening rate, so managers should treat the modeled reductions as relative guidance and re-estimate with airport-specific arrival data before capital commits. The abandonment/re-entry patience model is an approximation, and the cultural archetypes are stylized proxies for traveler-style variation rather than measured ethnic/cultural groups.
